summary:
The federal Self-Determination Act (Selbstbestimmungsgesetz, SBGG) governs legal gender recognition in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern as in every other German Land. Approved by the federal cabinet in August 2023, passed by the Bundestag in April 2024 by 374 votes to 251, and in force since 1 November 2024, it allows adults over 18 to change their legal first name and gender entry by self-declaration with three months' notice and no medical certification. No Mecklenburg-Vorpommern-specific trans statute, ordinance or placement reform is recorded in the sources; the federal framework applies here in full.

Prison placement is the sharpest documented exposure in this Land. Under the Self-Determination Act, placement follows the prisoner's legal gender entry unless state law provides otherwise, and Länder prison statutes may contain either abstract exception clauses or clauses targeting trans prisoners specifically; which form is legitimate is actively debated. In July 2026 the Landgericht Neubrandenburg, sitting in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, ordered that a prisoner be held in a men's prison despite a completed legal gender change. The case, known as the Liebich case and reported by France24 on 16 July 2026, prompted Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia to launch a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act.

Same-sex marriage with full marital and adoption rights has been available across Germany since 1 October 2017, under implementing legislation passed on 30 June 2017.
tangentialFactors:
The Neubrandenburg ruling sits within a wider Länder pattern of contested prison placement under the Self-Determination Act, analysed by Verfassungsblog on 18 March 2026, rather than as an isolated local decision.

The Liebich case has already produced a legislative response at federal level: three neighbouring Länder have moved to tighten the Act that governs recognition and placement in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, so the rules a visitor or resident relies on may be amended through the Bundesrat.
localsOnly:
Residents of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern seeking to change their legal name or gender entry do so under the federal self-declaration procedure, with three months' notice and no medical evidence required; the sources record no separate state procedure or additional local hurdle.

People held in custody in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern face the placement rule applied in the Neubrandenburg case: a completed legal gender change did not prevent a men's prison assignment, and the state's courts have shown willingness to order placement against the legal gender entry.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Mecklenburg-Vorpommern's own correctional statute contains an abstract or a trans-targeted exception clause, and how intake placement is decided in practice at facilities in this Land, is not resolved in the sources beyond the July 2026 Neubrandenburg ruling.

No region-specific data on hate-crime reporting, hate-crime incidents, access to gender-affirming care, or facilities and venue access in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern is sourced here; those layers are not established by this inventory.
